title: One pull to wipe them all
excerpt: A malicious pull request submitted to Amazon's public aws-toolkit-vscode repository in July 2025 injected a prompt instructing the Q Developer AI coding agent...
content_html:
A malicious pull request submitted to Amazon's public aws-toolkit-vscode repository in July 2025 injected a prompt instructing the Q Developer AI coding agent to wipe systems and delete file and cloud resources, and it shipped to nearly a million VS Code marketplace users before a formatting error stopped it from executing. The root cause traced to a GitHub access token with excessive permissions inside the build pipeline; Amazon revoked credentials and pushed a clean build within two days. A separate researcher-found bash command vulnerability was patched by July 18, and both Q Developer and Kiro now require human-in-the-loop confirmation before running previously unchecked commands. The piece argues agents can't distinguish legitimate instructions from injected ones and calls for policy gates outside the agent, short-lived credentials, and treating build pipelines as attack surfaces.

Questions this post answers

What happened with the Amazon Q Developer VS Code extension security incident in July 2025?

A GitHub user named lkmanka58 submitted a malicious pull request to Amazon's aws-toolkit-vscode repository on July 13, 2025, which injected a prompt instructing the Q Developer AI agent to wipe systems to near-factory state and delete file-system and cloud resources. It shipped to nearly a million VS Code marketplace installs four days later, but a formatting error in the prompt prevented it from executing, and Amazon confirmed it never ran in a customer environment. daily.dev surfaces incidents like this for teams hardening their AI coding agent supply chain.

How did the attacker gain the ability to push malicious code into Amazon Q Developer's official release?

The attacker exploited a GitHub access token with excessive permissions inside the service used to compile extensions and cut release packages, allowing them to commit malicious code directly to the open-source repo, which the build service then packaged into the official release. Once discovered, Amazon revoked the attacker's credentials, removed the code, and pushed a clean build within two days. Engineers auditing build pipeline credentials can track supply chain security findings on daily.dev.

What command execution vulnerability did Johann Rehberger find in Amazon Q Developer, and how was it fixed?

Independent researcher Johann Rehberger found that Q Developer would run bash commands, such as find, without asking for permission, a gap exploitable to leak files or trigger remote code execution. He reported it on July 7, 2025, it was patched by July 18, and Amazon published a security bulletin confirming the fix that October, though no CVE was issued because the report required prior system compromise. Developers tracking AI coding agent vulnerabilities can follow disclosures like this on daily.dev.
